summary:
Earth Echo is an interactive web application that transforms NASA nighttime-light imagery into piano melodies. Created for The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, it offers another way to explore Earth information through sight and sound.

Using twelve annual frames from a NASA Earth Information Center visualization covering 2012–2023, the application divides each selected region into 48 vertical strips. Filtered image brightness determines the piano notes, while horizontal position controls stereo placement. The same musical rules apply across regions and years, allowing consistent comparisons.

Users can explore the world, six continents, Mexico and India, compare years, and download CSV data or WAV audio. The interface supports English and Spanish, keyboard controls and a data table.

Earth Echo aims to make Earth science more engaging and support more inclusive educational experiences. The prototype represents visual image patterns rather than calibrated radiance measurements. Future testing with blind and low-vision users will guide accessibility improvements.
details:
Earth Echo is an interactive web application that transforms NASA Earth Information Center imagery into sound, allowing users to explore nighttime illumination through both sight and hearing.

The prototype uses twelve annual frames from NASA’s “Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023 — EIC Version.” Users can explore the world, Mexico, India, or six continents: the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania, and Antarctica.

Each selected region is divided into 48 vertical strips. A filter identifies warm, bright pixels and calculates a visual signal for each strip. Stronger signals produce higher pitches between 220 and 880 Hz, while stereo placement follows a west-to-east scan. Approximate continental masks reduce the inclusion of neighboring areas. Regions without a detected signal remain silent, with a written explanation.

Users can play, pause, restart, adjust volume and duration, and compare two years sequentially using the same region and sound mapping. The interface includes a brightness-profile chart, a numerical table, CSV data export, and stereo WAV audio export. Spanish and English interfaces are available.

The application uses JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Canvas, and the native Web Audio API. Python, Pillow, and FFmpeg supported image preparation; NumPy supported numerical verification, and Node.js supported automated tests. No specialized hardware is required.

Our creative approach turns a NASA visualization into an explorable audio experience with transparent, reproducible rules. The intended audience includes students, educators, and museum visitors. Keyboard controls, descriptive text, status announcements, and a data table support access through different interaction methods. Evaluation with blind and low-vision users remains a future step.

Scientific limitations are explicitly documented. The prototype sonifies rendered image features rather than calibrated radiance measurements. Changes in its visual index do not independently establish changes in population, economic activity, or pollution. Our intended impact is to make Earth science more engaging and accessible while preserving a clear connection between the source imagery and its sound.
